#### 9.5.1 Null Hypothesis and Alternative Hypothesis
The null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) represents the default assumption that there is no significant difference or effect between a test case and its corresponding baseline implementation.
The alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)), on the other hand, suggests that there is a significant effect.

#### 9.5.2 Type I Error (False Positive)
Type I error occurs when we reject \(H_0\) (the null hypothesis) when it is actually true.

#### 9.5.3 Type II Error (False Negative)
In contrast, a type II error occurs when we fail to reject \(H_0\) (the null hypothesis) even though \(H_1\) is true.

#### 9.5.4 Significance Level (\(\alpha\))
The significance level \(\alpha\) is a threshold set by researchers that determines how likely they are willing to accept a Type I error (the probability of incorrectly rejecting \(H_0\)).
Commonly, \(\alpha = 0.05\) or 5%, meaning there's a 5% chance of committing a type I error.

#### 9.5.5 Power (\(1 - \beta\))
The power of the test is the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when it is false (\(\beta\) represents Type II error).

#### 9.5.6 Confidence Intervals (CI)

For example, if an SPE system is evaluated with a 90% confidence level, it means there's a 10% chance that the actual difference between two implementations falls outside this calculated range.

#### 9.5.7 Central Limit Theorem
The central limit theorem states that regardless of the population distribution, the sampling distribution of the mean will approximate a normal distribution as the sample size increases.

#### 9.5.8 P-Value
A p-value is the probability of observing the test statistic or something more extreme if \(H_0\) were true.
If a calculated p-value is below the significance level \(\alpha\), we reject \(H_0\).
